title: Could You Live to 200? (Lessons From a Whale)
description: What if one of the greatest secrets extending human life has been hiding inside the largest animals on Earth? It’s the bowhead whale. These creatures can live 250 years, which means there are bowheads around today that were born before the light bulb was invented. They can weigh more than 200,000 pounds, and have mouths large enough to fit an entire SUV. But I’m not telling you about this extraordinary creature simply because of its immense size or incredible longevity. I’m telling you about it because of a biological paradox that may help explain how it lives so long. Something you’ve probably never thought about. Something we could use. These whales should be riddled with tumors. But they aren’t. Think about it. Every time a cell divides, it has to copy its DNA. And every time DNA is copied, there’s a chance of making a mistake that could ultimately lead to cancer. Now consider that this whale has roughly a 1000-times more cells than a human, and some those cells divide for centuries. More cells. More cell divisions. More opportunities for cancer-causing mutations. These whales should be swimming tumors! And yet, they appear remarkably resistant to cancer. So what’s their secret? And more importantly, could we harness that secret to protect ourselves from cancer, and even extend human lifespans far beyond what we currently imagine possible? Scientists are beginning to think we might.

title: How To Destroy Visceral Fat (Proven in 4 RCTs)
description: You can demolish your visceral fat dramatically within a matter of weeks. And you can do it without cutting calories. I’m going to prove it to you, drawing from multiple human randomized controlled trials, and sharing tools you can start using immediately. But before we get to the “ how-to, ” we need to determine the “ why. ” Why would you want to eviscerate visceral fat? Because not all fat is created equal. Subcutaneous fat (the type that sits under your skin) has important physiological functions. It provides insulation, and maintaining a modest amount helps support hormonal health. But visceral fat is different… Visceral Fat and Heart Health V isceral fat surrounds your internal organs, releases inflammatory molecules, and increases your risk of cardiovascular disease. For example, in the landmark INTERHEART study , involving approximately 27,000 participants across 52 countries, individuals in the highest quintile of waist-to-hip ratio (a proxy for visceral fat) had 2.5 times the odds of having a heart attack compared with those in the lowest quintile. Importantly, this association was substantially stronger than that observed with BMI, highlighting that where you store fat matters more for cardiovascular risk than how much you weigh. Visceral Fat and Brain Health Elevated visceral fat is also strongly linked to cognitive decline and dementia. Recent research out of Harvard suggests that the greater your cumulative exposure to visceral fat, the faster your brain shrinks as you age. So, visceral fat doesn't just expand your waistline. It also downsizes your brain. Talk about a terrible trade deal. We’ll dive into that fascinating science behind this in a moment. But first, here’s a 41-second video preview of what we’re about to explore.

title: What Should You Do When the Evidence Runs Out? (Short Read)
description: When I was 22, my life was just taking off and crumbling at the same time. It was “taking off” because I had achieved everything I had wanted to achieve academically by that age. I had just graduated valedictorian from my college, moved to Oxford to complete my PhD, and had a place secured at Harvard Medical School to complete my MD thereafter. I grew up in medicine. Both my parents were physician-scientists, and this path was always what I wanted. But my life was also crumbling because, at the same time, I was struggling with a debilitating case of inflammatory bowel disease. Instead of spending my days in the lab, I was often in a hospital bed. The flares became so severe that I regularly required intensive treatment, and the malnourishment was so profound that my heart would sometimes flutter in the 20s. The promise I had on paper was an empty promise because my health was slipping away. It’s a truly dark irony. A family of doctors, a doctor in training, all the resources one could have, and yet the best evidence-based medicine wasn’t helping me. After some years, when medication stopped having control over the disease and we began discussing what life without a colon would look like, I went searching for alternative solutions in desperation. I wanted to know whether maybe the food passing through my gut every day would have any effect on the disease of my gut. The answer came back in five concrete words: “There is no good evidence.” There is no good evidence that dietary change could put my disease into remission. When the Evidence Runs Out So, I started to collect my own evidence, the humblest form of evidence: the N=1 experiment. I started trying things myself. Things that, by conventional standards, would be considered fringe.
